payload.theorem_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, ℓ with 0 ≤ k, ℓ ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose ℓ]_q is a polynomial in q, then it has only nonnegative coefficients.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix n, k, l and assume the Gaussian quotient is a polynomial. First use symmetry to replace k and l by a = min(k, n-k) and b = min(l, n-l) without changing the quotient. A degree comparison then forces 0 <= b <= a <= n/2. Next rewrite the reduced quotient as the normalized consecutive product P_{a,b,c}(q) with c = n-a-b >= 0. Cyclotomic factorization expresses polynomiality of P_{a,b,c}(q) as a family of interval-divisibility inequalities: every modulus d occurs at least as often in the shifted numerator interval {c+b+1, ..., c+a} as in the denominator interval {b+1, ..., a}. The only substantive remaining task is the bottleneck positivity theorem L5, which asserts that any normalized interval product satisfying these inequalities has nonnegative coefficients. Applying that theorem to P_{a,b,c}(q) gives coefficientwise nonnegativity, and the earlier equalities transport the conclusion back to the original quotient [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q.

steps.derives: Fix integers n, k, l with 0 <= k <= n and 0 <= l <= n, and assume Q(q) := [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial. Let a := min(k, n-k) and b := min(l, n-l). Then [n choose k]_q = [n choose a]_q and [n choose l]_q = [n choose b]_q, so Q(q) = [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q. In particular, the reduced quotient [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q is also a polynomial.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L1 once with r = k and once with r = l. Replacing numerator and denominator by equal Gaussian coefficients does not change the quotient, so the original and reduced quotients are identical as rational functions. Since the original quotient is assumed polynomial, the reduced quotient is polynomial as well.

steps.derives: The reduced indices satisfy 0 <= b <= a <= n/2.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the conclusion of L2 for the same n, k, l, a, and b under the standing polynomiality assumption.

steps.derives: If c := n-a-b, then c >= 0 and [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q = P_{a,b,c}(q) := product_{i=b+1}^a (1-q^(c+i))/(1-q^i). Hence Q(q) = P_{a,b,c}(q).
steps.trivial_justification: From A2, a <= n/2 and b >= 0, so c = n-a-b is nonnegative. Lemma L3 rewrites the reduced quotient as the stated consecutive-factor product. Combining this with A1 identifies the original quotient Q(q) with P_{a,b,c}(q).

steps.derives: For every positive integer d, the interval {c+b+1, ..., c+a} contains at least as many multiples of d as the interval {b+1, ..., a}.
steps.trivial_justification: By A1 and A3, P_{a,b,c}(q) equals the reduced quotient and is therefore a polynomial. Applying L4 to this polynomial gives the explicit cyclotomic-exponent formula and its consequence: for each d > 0, the multiplicity count in the shifted interval {c+b+1, ..., c+a} is at least the multiplicity count in {b+1, ..., a}.

steps.derives: Every coefficient of P_{a,b,c}(q) is nonnegative.
steps.trivial_justification: A4 gives exactly the arithmetic hypothesis required by L5, so L5 directly yields coefficientwise nonnegativity of P_{a,b,c}(q).

steps.derives: Therefore the quotient [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q has only nonnegative coefficients whenever it is a polynomial in q. This is exactly the theorem: for all integers n, k, l with 0 <= k, l <= n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then every coefficient of that polynomial is nonnegative.
steps.trivial_justification: Step A5 proves coefficientwise nonnegativity for P_{a,b,c}(q). Step A3 identifies P_{a,b,c}(q) with the reduced quotient [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q, and Step A1 identifies that reduced quotient with the original quotient [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q. Substituting these equalities transfers the nonnegativity conclusion back to the original quotient, yielding exactly the root statement.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let a, b, and c be integers with 0 <= b <= a and c >= 0. Define P_{a,b,c}(q) := product_{i=b+1}^a (1-q^(c+i))/(1-q^i), with the empty product equal to 1 when a = b. Let Phi_d(q) denote the d-th cyclotomic polynomial, characterized by q^m - 1 = product_{d | m} Phi_d(q). Then for every positive integer d, the exponent of Phi_d(q) in the cyclotomic factorization of the rational function P_{a,b,c}(q) equals #{x in {c+b+1, ..., c+a} : d divides x} - #{x in {b+1, ..., a} : d divides x}. In particular, if P_{a,b,c}(q) is a polynomial in q, then for every positive integer d the interval {c+b+1, ..., c+a} contains at least as many multiples of d as the interval {b+1, ..., a}.
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: This is cyclotomic bookkeeping: it computes factor exponents but does not address coefficient signs.

candidates.strategy_summary: Reduce by symmetry to indices a = min(k, n-k) and b = min(l, n-l) with 0 <= b <= a <= n/2, rewrite the quotient as a consecutive interval product product_{i=b+1}^a (1-q^(c+i))/(1-q^i) with c = n-a-b, convert polynomiality into nonnegative cyclotomic multiplicities via interval-count inequalities, and isolate the genuine difficulty as a positivity theorem for these normalized interval products. The bottleneck lemma is a clean arithmetic positivity statement that can be attacked independently, for example by Christoffel-path or Hilbert-series methods.
